summary:
We developed Sol 30: Mars Outpost Commander, a free browser game for ages 7 to 12. The player runs a Mars outpost for 30 sols and must keep four astronauts alive by sharing a small power budget between air, a greenhouse, a storm shield and a workshop that builds upgrades. There is never enough power for everything.

It addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real mission trade-offs into decisions a child can make. Every mission replays a real month of the Sun: solar eruptions come from NASA’s DONKI database, and the Curiosity rover’s radiation readings decide whether a storm really reached Mars. When a mission ends early, a debrief explains the trade-off behind it and what to try next.

It matters because future explorers will need to make hard choices with real data, not only memorise facts. Sol 30 needs no download or account, and its missions work offline, so children can start training with nothing more than a browser.
details:
What it does and how it works

Sol 30: Mars Outpost Commander is a browser game for ages 7 to 12. The player commands a Mars outpost for 30 sols and must keep four astronauts alive. Each sol they read the morning news, share out 9 units of power between life support, a greenhouse, a storm shield and a workshop, then press Run Sol. Air and food for the crew take 8 of the 9, so a shield or an upgrade has to be paid for out of the air tank or the pantry. The mission ends early if the air runs out, the crew goes hungry three sols in a row, or storm radiation passes the limit.

Every mission replays a real 30-day window. Solar eruptions come from NASA’s DONKI database, the Curiosity rover’s radiation readings (NASA RadLab) decide whether a storm really reached Mars and how big it was, and seven studies from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository appear as science cards on the end screen.

Benefits

There is no download, account or backend, and the missions work offline. When a mission fails, a debrief explains which trade-off caused it and what to try next, and always says the crew flew home safely, so children are encouraged to try again.

Intended impact

We want children to practise the thinking real missions need: planning ahead, weighing risks, and deciding with uncertain data. They come to win a game and leave having read real NASA science.

Tools and technology

TypeScript, HTML and CSS, built with Vite

Vitest for 75 automated tests on the rules, the data and the balance

A Node.js script that builds the archived NASA data snapshot

NASA’s DONKI API for the live “Check the Sun today” button

GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for testing and publishing

No special hardware: any device with a modern browser

Creativity

It isn’t a quiz about space. Real solar history is the level design: six real months, from a quiet December 2019 to the storm of May 2024, the biggest Curiosity has measured. Most warnings miss Mars, as in the real data, so players learn to judge risk rather than follow a rule.

Factors we considered

Honesty: a Sources panel tells players what is real NASA data and what is a game rule.

Fairness: automated players run 40 missions per month to check that careful play can win, careless play can lose, and no fixed strategy always wins.

Age: plain language, large buttons, text labels and reduced-motion support.

Tone: no one dies; every early ending brings the crew home.

Access: offline play, so a weak connection is not a barrier.
